## AI Automation Society Newsletter

**Priority: MEDIUM**

### Top Updates
* The AI Automation Society is hosting a Q&A session with Nate on Monday, August 3rd, at 7:30pm - 8:00pm Calcutta time, which is open to plus members and will be recorded, providing an opportunity for members to engage with Nate and gain insights into AI automation.
* The AI Automation Society has recently surpassed 100,000 members and over 2,000 paying "Plus" subscribers, positioning it as a significant grassroots ecosystem around applied AI agents and automation businesses, and contributing to the broader diffusion of AI automation capabilities into traditional industries.
* The community has announced its first hackathon, launching August 1 with $6,000 in total prizes and a dedicated beginner track aimed at accelerating learning and project-building for new members, which highlights the community's focus on practical application and innovation in AI automation.
* The AI Automation Society operates as an informal workforce development and innovation network for AI automation, helping to seed more small-scale AI agencies and independent builders who implement AI/ML tools in real businesses, thereby amplifying the practical impact of frontier models and agent frameworks across sectors.
* Skool.com, the platform hosting the AI Automation Society, has rolled out platform-level AI moderation combined with a 24/7 moderation team to manage content and community safety at scale, and has announced that discovery and distribution are its #1 focus, with over 1 million people searching Skool daily to find communities.
* Link.skool.com functions as a custom URL shortener and tracking layer used by Skool to route traffic into specific Skool communities, sign-up flows, and promotional funnels, supporting the growth and tracking infrastructure for AI education and automation communities.

### Notable Links
* [AI Automation Society](https://www.skool.com/ai-automation-society)
* [Skool.com](https://www.skool.com)
* Link.skool.com

additionalContext.context:
AI Automation Society is a large online community and education platform focused on AI agents, automation, and building AI-powered businesses, hosted primarily on Skool and grown out of YouTube content and resources shared by its founder starting in October 2024.[2] It functions as a hub for practitioners, freelancers, and entrepreneurs who want to learn how to design, deploy, and monetize AI automation systems, offering free community content alongside a paid "Plus" membership that adds structured curriculum, live sessions, and more advanced resources.[2][1]

It matters in the AI/ML space because it has rapidly become one of the more active practitioner communities: according to its own updates, the group recently surpassed 100,000 members and over 2,000 paying "Plus" subscribers, positioning it as a significant grassroots ecosystem around applied AI agents and automation businesses rather than purely academic or research-focused AI.[2] The community’s emphasis on sales pipelines, client acquisition, and real-world automation projects makes it a training ground for AI consultants and agency owners who help SMEs and startups implement AI workflows, contributing to the broader diffusion of AI automation capabilities into traditional industries.[2][5]

Recent developments include the announcement of the Society’s first hackathon, launching August 1 with $6,000 in total prizes and a dedicated beginner track aimed at accelerating learning and project-building for new members.[2] The group also continues to run live events such as "AIS Live" and themed sessions (e.g., "Behind the Build" and "The Modern AI Sales Pipeline"), and it has achieved recognition within the Skool platform by winning back-to-back Skool Games competitions, including Q1 and Q2 titles that highlight high engagement and course completion within its community.[1][2] From an industry impact perspective, AI Automation Society operates as an informal workforce development and innovation network for AI automation, helping to seed more small-scale AI agencies and independent builders who implement AI/ML tools in real businesses, thereby amplifying the practical impact of frontier models and agent frameworks across sectors.

Skool is an online community and course platform that powers large, niche-focused groups like the **AI Automation Society**, which is hosted as a Skool community and described as a place to “learn to get paid for AI solutions, regardless of your background.”[1][6] In the AI/ML space, Skool functions less as a model or tool provider and more as an infrastructure layer for education, collaboration, and community-building around applied AI, enabling creators and organizations to run structured programs, live events, and resource libraries for people learning to build AI-powered workflows and businesses.[1][6][7]

The AI Automation Society community on Skool has grown rapidly, with recent third-party tracking showing membership in the hundreds of thousands and daily net growth in the hundreds of new members, indicating strong demand for practical AI automation training and peer support.[3][9] Within the community, organizers run live events like **AIS Live** and publish resources such as long-form courses (e.g., a multi-hour “Claude Code for Non-Coders” training) and implementation-focused content on AI agents and automation systems.[1][5][8][9] This positions Skool as a significant distribution and engagement channel for AI/ML education, giving practitioners a structured environment to move from general AI interest to deploying automation solutions in real businesses, and contributing to the broader industry trend of community-driven, practice-oriented AI upskilling.[1][3][8][9]

In the current AI/ML landscape, **AI automation** refers to the use of increasingly autonomous AI agents and models to *execute tasks end-to-end*, not just generate text or predictions.[8][10] This includes systems that can plan, call tools and APIs, interact with enterprise software, and iteratively improve their own workflows, effectively acting as digital workers across domains like software development, operations, marketing, finance, and customer support.[4][8][10] The focus has shifted from standalone models to **agentic architectures** and orchestration layers that enable AI to perform multi-step processes with minimal human intervention.[4][8][10]

It matters because it is rapidly transforming productivity and operating models in both tech and traditional industries. Enterprises are deploying AI agents to automate email and document workflows (e.g., Google's Gemini Spark for Gmail/Drive), customer interactions, and complex supply chain and manufacturing tasks, such as Huawei’s AI models optimizing steel production and Hershey applying AI across sourcing and fulfillment.[1][5][8] Major AI labs and cloud providers are racing to provide agent-ready platforms—OpenAI’s workplace-focused agents (ChatGPT Work), Google’s agentic integrations in AI Mode, and SAP/Google Cloud’s agentic commerce architecture—aimed at automating marketing, retail, and back-office operations at scale.[1][4][8][10] At the systems level, new infrastructure and tools (e.g., MCP for stateless session handling, AgentDebugX for agent observability, DataFlow-Harness for code agents managing data pipelines) are emerging to make large-scale **agent deployments** more reliable and secure.[10]

The latest developments center on three trends: (1) **more capable models and specialized agents** for automation, such as Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 and related AI automation features, Google DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve for autonomous code writing and testing, and new GPT-5.6 tiers optimized for coding and agent tasks.[8][10] (2) **enterprise and sectoral rollouts**, with companies like SAP, HP, and Hershey integrating AI agents deeply into workflows, and governments and regulators (e.g., the Bank of England, UN digital tech agency) examining rules and trust frameworks for agentic AI in finance and other critical domains.[1][4] (3) **risk, governance, and evaluation tooling**, as prompt-injection flaws, sandbox misconfigurations, and privacy leaks in agentic workflows highlight the need for observability, trajectory-level QA (AgentLens), and formal testbeds such as AgenticSTS.[7][10] Collectively, these advances signal that AI automation is moving from experimental pilots to core infrastructure—reshaping labor, software development, and business processes, while raising new issues around oversight, security, and competition in the AI ecosystem.[1][4][8][9][10]

Skool.com is a **community and course platform** designed for creators, educators, and niche experts to build paid and free learning communities that combine discussion, gamification, and structured courses in one place.[2][3] It has increasingly become a hub for AI, ML, and automation-focused groups, with specialized communities like the **AI Agent Innovation Academy**, AI Automation Society, and various AI marketing and automation programs using Skool as their primary delivery and collaboration environment.[1][2][3][9] This positioning makes Skool relevant in the AI/ML space as an infrastructure layer for practitioners and businesses who are operationalizing AI through education, cohort-based programs, and community-led implementation.[1][2][3]

The platform’s recent developments show a clear strategic focus on **discovery, distribution, and AI-powered features** that directly impact AI/ML ecosystems using Skool. In 2025, Skool rolled out **platform-level AI moderation** combined with a 24/7 moderation team to manage content and community safety at scale, indicating the use of AI for trust, safety, and automation.[8] In 2026, Skool announced that **discovery and distribution are its #1 focus**, with over **1 million people searching Skool daily** to find communities, supported by a new discovery algorithm, improved search, ranking, and category systems, plus trending filters to help AI and other niche communities get found more easily.[6][7][10] These discovery upgrades, along with roadmap items such as multi-language and multi-currency support, signal Skool’s intent to be a global marketplace-like environment where AI/ML communities can attract, convert, and retain members at scale.[6][7]

In the AI/ML industry context, Skool’s impact comes less from building foundational models and more from enabling **distribution, education, and implementation** of AI solutions via specialized communities. AI-focused programs on Skool use the platform to teach agent-based automation, AI employees, AI marketing systems, and AI-driven business workflows, which accelerates practical adoption of AI among entrepreneurs and operators.[1][2][3][5][9][10] The closure of some earlier AI-focused communities like the Skool AI Masterclass shows the ecosystem is evolving, with newer, more targeted AI communities replacing legacy ones.[4][9] Overall, Skool.com matters in the AI/ML space as a rapidly-growing, discovery-optimized community platform where AI educators and automation experts organize cohorts, share playbooks, and scale AI literacy and deployment across non-technical and business audiences.[1][2][3][6][7][8][9][10]

Link.skool.com appears to function as a **custom URL shortener and tracking layer** used by Skool, the online community and course platform, to route traffic into specific Skool communities, sign‑up flows, and promotional funnels.[1][5] Rather than being a standalone AI/ML product, it is an infrastructure tool that supports Skool’s broader ecosystem of niche communities, many of which focus heavily on AI, automation, and related technologies.[2][3][4][5][7] In practice, creators and community owners share shortened links (including Skool’s own referral and signup links) to direct users into AI-focused groups such as School of AI, AI Lab, and various AI automation societies hosted on Skool.[3][4][5][7] 

Its relevance in the AI/ML space comes from Skool’s rapid growth as a **hub for AI and automation communities**, not from Link.skool.com offering core AI functionality itself.[5] Recent analyses of Skool’s community landscape show that four of the five largest communities on the entire platform are in the Tech/AI category, many explicitly focused on AI automation, AI for LinkedIn, and AI-powered content creation.[2][3][4][5][7] These communities use Skool’s links and referral mechanisms (including shortened or branded URLs) to scale membership, distribute AI courses and bootcamps, and coordinate experiments with AI-driven workflows, making Link.skool.com part of the underlying growth and tracking infrastructure for this AI ecosystem rather than a headline AI product.[5][6]

From an industry-impact standpoint, Link.skool.com is best understood as **supporting infrastructure for AI education and automation communities**: it helps creators measure and optimize traffic into AI-focused groups, paid memberships, and bootcamps that teach applied AI skills like automation, content generation, and AI-assisted marketing.[3][4][5][6][7][9] As more AI communities aggregate on Skool and share referral-based links in newsletters, YouTube descriptions, and social posts, Link.skool.com and related Skool link mechanisms quietly contribute to distribution, engagement tracking, and monetization of AI/ML knowledge, but there is no public indication that Link.skool.com itself introduces novel AI algorithms or ML features beyond standard link management.[1][5][9]

missingStories.headline: Microsoft launches Copilot 3D for instant AI-generated 3D assets
missingStories.summary: Microsoft released Copilot 3D, a new AI tool that can generate usable 3D models directly from text prompts, integrating with existing Copilot and design workflows.[2][8] The launch targets game development, AR/VR, and digital content creators needing rapid asset generation.[2][8]
missingStories.whyItMatters: Copilot 3D significantly lowers the barrier to creating 3D content, opening up new pipelines for simulation, gaming, and spatial computing applications. AI practitioners working on graphics, digital twins, and mixed reality can now integrate text-to-3D generation into their toolchains, shifting more value from manual modeling to model orchestration and asset refinement.
missingStories.source: Microsoft Copilot 3D launch coverage in recent AI news roundup video

missingStories.headline: Perplexity rolls out AI video generation for Pro & Max subscribers
missingStories.summary: Perplexity introduced an AI video generation capability for its paid tiers, enabling users to produce short, information-dense videos from prompts or documents.[2] The feature extends Perplexity’s answer engine into multimodal content creation for education, communication, and marketing use cases.[2]
missingStories.whyItMatters: This marks a further convergence of search, reasoning, and media generation, giving practitioners a production-ready tool that turns textual knowledge into video artifacts. It also highlights a broader trend: LLM-based assistants evolving into full content studios, which affects how AI products are designed, monetized, and integrated into workflows.
missingStories.source: Perplexity AI video generation feature announcement highlighted in AI news roundup

missingStories.headline: Nvidia unveils Neotron 3 family of foundation models
missingStories.summary: Nvidia released a new family of models branded Neotron 3, aimed at high‑performance AI workloads including code, language, and multimodal tasks.[8] These models are optimized for Nvidia’s GPU stack and are positioned as broadly deployable foundation models for enterprises and developers.[8]
missingStories.whyItMatters: A new tier of vendor-optimized foundation models from Nvidia influences both infrastructure choices and model-selection strategies for practitioners. Tight integration with Nvidia GPUs can improve efficiency and cost profiles for large-scale training and inference, while also reinforcing the trend of hardware–model co-design that teams must account for in their architectures.
missingStories.source: Nvidia Neotron 3 model family coverage in recent AI headlines video

missingStories.headline: Microsoft releases Trellis 2 for image-to-3D model generation
missingStories.summary: Microsoft launched Trellis 2, an AI model that converts 2D images into detailed 3D models, advancing its spatial computing and design tooling.[8] Trellis 2 aims to streamline asset creation for industries like gaming, architecture, and product design by automating 3D reconstruction from existing imagery.[8]
missingStories.whyItMatters: Image-to-3D pipelines are critical for building virtual environments and digital twins at scale, and Trellis 2 brings this capability closer to mainstream developer tooling. AI practitioners can incorporate Trellis-style models into automated content creation workflows, reducing reliance on manual 3D modeling and enabling new applications in simulation, robotics, and XR.
missingStories.source: Microsoft Trellis 2 announcement reported in AI news recap

missingStories.headline: Global leaders warn of AI risks and governance gaps at Summer Davos
missingStories.summary: At the Summer Davos gathering, policymakers and business leaders emphasized that the world risks 'losing control of technology' without stronger AI governance frameworks.[10] Discussions focused on balancing AI-driven economic opportunity with systemic risks, including misuse, concentration of power, and cross-border regulatory fragmentation.[10]
missingStories.whyItMatters: For AI practitioners, this signals increasing political momentum toward stricter oversight and potentially binding global or regional frameworks on safety, transparency, and accountability. Teams building and deploying models will need to anticipate compliance requirements, documentation standards, and alignment with emerging international norms around responsible AI.
missingStories.source: Coverage of AI governance discussions and warnings at Summer Davos from global news outlets
